abstract.t: This document specifies GSS-SSHKEY, a GSS-API security mechanism that establishes a security context using SSH public keys. The mechanism performs an ephemeral key exchange, authenticates the acceptor with an SSH host key, authenticates the initiator with an SSH user key, and derives per-message keys for GSS-API protection.
This is an experimental specification. The mechanism OID used here is allocated from a private enterprise arc for implementation experiments and is not suitable for final publication.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Overview
section.t: GSS-SSHKEY is a peer authentication and key establishment protocol for the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) . It reuses SSH public-key identities and signature algorithms while presenting the result as an ordinary GSS-API security context.

The initiator is the user side of the exchange. The acceptor is the service or host side. The acceptor proves possession of a trusted SSH host private key. After a shared session secret can be derived, the initiator proves possession of an SSH user private key in an encrypted user-authentication payload. Both peers then prove knowledge of the derived session key.

Context-establishment tokens are DER encodings of the ASN.1 SshKeyToken type defined in . Per-message tokens use the GSS-API CFX token framing described in , with keys derived by this mechanism instead of by Kerberos.

The SASL mechanism name for use by implementations that expose a SASL name is "SSHKEY".

section.name: Names and Credentials
section.t: The target name supplied to gss_init_sec_context() SHOULD be a host-based service name. The service component identifies the application service, and the host component identifies the SSH host key namespace in which the acceptor key is validated.

The acceptor credential consists of one or more SSH host private keys and their public-key metadata. The initiator credential consists of SSH user keys available through an SSH agent. A GSS mechanism implementation normally cannot prompt for SSH private-key passphrases, so initiator implementations of this mechanism MUST NOT depend on direct user interaction to unlock private key files.

An implementation MUST define how trusted acceptor host public keys are found. Implementations MUST support OpenSSH known_hosts style host-key databases and MUST support SSHFP DNS resource records. SSHFP records MUST be treated as authentic only when the DNS answer is DNSSEC validated. A deployment MAY additionally use a certificate authority or another local trust store. This protocol does not make unauthenticated host keys trustworthy.

section.name: Token Encoding
section.t: All context-establishment tokens exchanged by gss_init_sec_context() and gss_accept_sec_context() are DER encodings of SshKeyToken. Implementations MUST reject tokens that are not valid DER encodings of that type.

Algorithm-list fields are OCTET STRING values containing SSH name-lists as defined by . Algorithm name fields are OCTET STRING values containing one SSH algorithm name. Signature blobs are encoded as SSH binary strings as used by and .
Encrypted OCTET STRING fields contain an SSH binary packet with the following fields:
section.sourcecode: string enctype string nonce string ciphertext
section.t: For an AEAD enctype, ciphertext includes the authentication tag in the enctype-defined form. The associated data is the DER encoding of the enclosing SshKeyToken with the encrypted OCTET STRING value replaced by an empty OCTET STRING, followed by the signature transcript fields defined in .

section.name: Algorithm Negotiation
section.t: The kextypes, enctypes, and sigtypes fields carry the initiator's supported key-exchange, encryption, and SSH signature algorithms. The acceptor selects one key-exchange and encryption algorithm, and returns its own sigtypes list naming the user signature algorithms it is willing to verify. The actual host and user signature algorithms are carried in hostauth.sigtype and SshKeyUserAuth.sigtype.
SSH public key type and SSH signature type are negotiated separately. This is necessary for RSA, where one ssh-rsa public key can produce rsa-sha2-512, rsa-sha2-256, or legacy ssh-rsa signatures.

Implementations of this draft SHOULD support curve25519-sha256 for key exchange, aes256-gcm-sha256 for encrypted fields and per-message tokens, and ssh-ed25519 for signatures. Curve25519 is described in .
This mechanism is new and has no compatibility requirement for Kerberos DES, Triple-DES, RC4, or other legacy RFC 4121 encryption types.

section.name: Signature Transcripts and Key Schedule
section.t: Signature inputs are encoded as SSH strings as defined by . In the initiator-first flow, the host signature input is:
section.sourcecode: SSH-string("gss-sshkey hostauth v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(kex-algorithm) || SSH-string(encryption-algorithm) || SSH-string(initiator-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(acceptor-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(initiator-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(acceptor-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(initiator-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-name) || SSH-string(channel-binding-application-data)
section.t: In the acceptor-first flow, the host challenge signature input is:
section.sourcecode: SSH-string("gss-sshkey hostchallenge v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(kex-algorithm) || SSH-string(encryption-algorithm) || SSH-string(acceptor-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(acceptor-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(acceptor-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-name) || SSH-string(channel-binding-application-data)
section.t: The user signature input is:
section.sourcecode: SSH-string("gss-sshkey userauth v1") || SSH-string(mechanism-oid-der-contents) || SSH-string(kex-algorithm) || SSH-string(encryption-algorithm) || SSH-string(initiator-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(acceptor-signature-algorithms) || SSH-string(initiator-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(acceptor-ecdh-public-key) || SSH-string(initiator-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-nonce) || SSH-string(acceptor-name) || SSH-string(username) || SSH-string(user-public-key-type) || SSH-string(user-public-key-blob) || SSH-string(user-signature-algorithm) || SSH-string(channel-binding-application-data)
section.t: EncSshKeyUserAuth is not tied to a single final user-authentication step. It MAY appear in any token sent after the sender has enough ECDH material to derive K_base. The encrypted payload lets initiator-first exchanges keep the username and user public key confidential from passive observers without adding a round trip.

Let Z be the raw shared secret produced by the selected key exchange. The anonymous ECDH profile derives the base session key with the same SP800-108 HMAC-SHA256 counter-mode KDF inputs as Heimdal SAnon-X25519:
section.sourcecode: K_base = KDF( K1 = Z, label = "sanon-x25519", context = initiator-pk || acceptor-pk || uint32(0) || uint32(flags) || channel-binding-application-data, L = 128 )
section.t: This version sends no SAnon-style optional protocol flags, so flags is zero. Directional per-message keys are derived from K_base using mechanism-specific HMAC-SHA256 labels. Nonces MUST NOT repeat for a given key and MUST include monotonically increasing sequence numbers.

Key confirmation uses a finished key derived from K_base and the transcript hash. SshKeyFinished.mac is an HMAC over a role label, the transcript hash, and the peer nonce. This proves possession of the ECDH-derived session key and does not require an additional SSH signature or SSH agent operation.

section.name: Initiator KEX Token
section.t: The first initiator token contains status SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED and a SshKeyKEX value. The kextypes, enctypes, and sigtypes fields contain the initiator algorithm lists. The kextype, enctype, and pk fields SHOULD contain the initiator's preferred proposal. The first initiator token SHOULD NOT contain EncSshKeyUserAuth, because the initiator cannot encrypt user authentication until it has received the acceptor ECDH public key.

section.name: Acceptor-First KEX Token
section.t: GSS-API does not require the initiator to generate the first context-establishment token. If the acceptor is called first with no input token, it sends SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED with SshKeyKEX, SshKeyHostAuth, and sctx. The token contains the acceptor's supported algorithms, preferred key-exchange public value, and a host-key signature over the acceptor-first challenge transcript.

The initiator response to an acceptor-first token contains its own SshKeyKEX value, EncSshKeyUserAuth, SshKeyFinished, and the reflected sctx. The acceptor uses sctx to recover its ephemeral ECDH state, derives the session key, decrypts the user authentication payload, validates the user signature, checks local authorization policy, and verifies the initiator finished MAC.

HTTP Negotiate is a natural acceptor-first deployment. An HTTP server MAY include an acceptor-first GSS-SSHKEY token in a 401 WWW-Authenticate header. The HTTP client can then return its ECDH public key, encrypted user authentication, key confirmation, and reflected sctx in the Authorization header. This lets the server authenticate the request during the normal HTTP authentication challenge round trip. If explicit acceptor key confirmation is required by the local implementation, the server can carry a final acceptor SshKeyFinished token in the HTTP response.

section.name: Acceptor KEX and Host Authentication Token
section.t: The acceptor validates the proposal, chooses algorithms, computes its key-exchange public value, and returns status SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED. The returned token contains SshKeyKEX with the selected algorithms and acceptor public value, and a SshKeyHostAuth value containing a hostauth signature.

In initiator-first exchanges, the acceptor can derive the session key after receiving the initiator public key. The acceptor token therefore MAY also contain SshKeyFinished. The initiator verifies the selected algorithms, hostauth.sig, and host-key trust policy before completing the context.

section.name: Encrypted User Authentication
section.t: Once the initiator has the acceptor ECDH public key, it derives the session keys, computes the user signature described in , DER encodes SshKeyUserAuth, encrypts it as EncSshKeyUserAuth, and sends it in the next token. The same token SHOULD contain the initiator SshKeyFinished value and MUST return sctx unchanged when sctx was present in the acceptor token.

section.name: Completion Token
section.t: The acceptor decrypts encuserauth, validates the SSH user signature, authorizes the requested username, verifies the initiator finished MAC, and returns SSH-KEY-COMPLETE. If the signature algorithm is not acceptable, the acceptor MAY return SSH-KEY-CONTINUE-NEEDED with sctx and a narrower sigtypes list. If validation, key confirmation, or authorization fails, the acceptor returns SSH-KEY-FAILURE.
A peer that receives SSH-KEY-FAILURE MUST fail context establishment and MUST discard all state derived from the failed exchange.

section.name: Context State Tokens
section.t: The cctx and sctx fields carry encrypted context state for implementations that need stateless initiator or acceptor operation. cctx is state intended for the initiator. sctx is state intended for the acceptor.

Context state MUST be confidentiality and integrity protected using keys unavailable to the peer that stores or reflects the state. Long-term private keys MUST NOT be stored in cctx or sctx. Context state SHOULD include the key-exchange transcript values and enough freshness data to prevent replay. For acceptor continuations, sctx MUST contain enough encrypted state for another acceptor process with the same context-protection key to finish authentication.
In the acceptor-first flow, sctx contains the acceptor's ephemeral ECDH private key until the initiator returns its public key. Long-term SSH host or user private keys MUST NOT be stored in sctx.

section.name: Per-Message Tokens
section.t: After SSH-KEY-COMPLETE, gss_get_mic(), gss_verify_mic(), gss_wrap(), and gss_unwrap() use CFX token framing . K_c2s protects initiator-to-acceptor tokens. K_s2c protects acceptor-to-initiator tokens. Sequence numbers start at zero in each direction. The token framing is from RFC 4121, but the encryption profile is aes256-gcm-sha256 rather than a Kerberos RFC 3961 encryption type.
A receiver MUST reject duplicate, reordered, or skipped tokens when the corresponding GSS-API replay or sequence flags were negotiated.

section.name: Error Handling
section.t: SSH-KEY-FAILURE is a generic protocol failure. A future version may define structured error codes. Until then, implementations SHOULD expose local diagnostic details through GSS minor status values rather than placing unauthenticated details on the wire.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This -00 draft requests no IANA action. Before publication as an RFC, the private experimental OID in must be replaced by a permanent GSS-API mechanism OID from an appropriate arc.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The security of this mechanism depends on correct validation of SSH host public keys and correct authorization of SSH user public keys. Implementations MUST NOT accept unknown host keys merely because they can verify hostauth.sig.

Signature inputs bind the algorithm lists, selected algorithms, and key-exchange public values. The finished MAC binds the derived session key to the same transcript. Omitting these values can permit downgrade, unknown-key-share, or key-confirmation failures.

EncSshKeyUserAuth hides the username, user public key, and user signature from passive observers. To reduce active identity probing, initiator implementations SHOULD validate the acceptor host signature and host-key trust policy before sending EncSshKeyUserAuth when that policy information is available locally. In all cases, implementations MUST NOT report a mutually authenticated context unless host-key policy succeeds.
All encrypted fields require nonce uniqueness. Reusing a nonce with an AEAD key can reveal plaintext and invalidate authentication.

Context state tokens are especially sensitive. They MUST be integrity protected, SHOULD be bound to the key-exchange transcript values, and SHOULD contain replay protection such as an expiration time or single-use state identifier.
This draft intentionally uses a private experimental OID. Deploying that OID outside controlled experiments risks collision with other private uses.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: The repository associated with this draft currently implements the mechanism loader interface, SAnon-compatible X25519 key derivation, SSH signature blob handling, encrypted acceptor continuation state, client-first and acceptor-first context establishment, RFC 4121-style per-message protection, and smoke tests that prove Heimdal can load the mechanism. The implementation has not yet caught up with this draft's authorized_keys authorization.

section.name: ASN.1 Module
section.t: This module is normative for context-establishment token syntax.
